questions.q: What does the **k** in k-means stand for?
options: The number of neighbours that vote on a label
The number of iterations the algorithm runs
The number of clusters, which you choose before running it
The number of features in the data
questions.why: In k-means, k is the number of groups (centroids) you ask for. "The number of neighbours that vote" describes k-NN, a supervised method that merely shares the letter k.

options: The number of points that switched cluster in the last round
The share of points correctly labelled
How far apart the different centroids are from each other
The total squared distance from every point to its own cluster's centroid
questions.why: Inertia (within-cluster sum of squares) is the number k-means tries to minimise; small inertia means tight clusters. It says nothing about separation between clusters, and there are no correct labels in unsupervised clustering.

questions.q: Run k-means with k = 2 on the numbers 1, 2, 4, 12, 14, starting with centroids at 1 and 2. After it converges, what is the inertia?
questions.why: First pass: {1} and {2, 4, 12, 14} with mean 8; then 2 and 4 move to the first cluster, giving {1, 2, 4} with mean 2.33 and {12, 14} with mean 13, after which nothing changes. Inertia = 1.78 + 0.11 + 2.78 + 1 + 1 ≈ 6.67. The tempting 5.33 adds plain (unsquared) distances; 2.00 counts only the big cluster.

questions.q: A customer's average distance to the rest of its own cluster is a = 2, and to the nearest other cluster b = 5. What is its silhouette value s = (b − a) / max(a, b)?
questions.why: s = (5 − 2) / 5 = 0.6, a comfortable fit with its own cluster. 0.4 is a / b, 2.5 is b / a (silhouette is always between −1 and +1), and a negative value would mean it sits closer to another cluster.

questions.q: Inertia for k = 1 to 6 is 1,000, 420, 180, 160, 145 and 135. What does the elbow method suggest?
options: k = 3, because after it extra clusters buy little improvement
k = 6, because it has the lowest inertia
k = 1, because inertia only goes down from there
No conclusion is possible without labels
questions.why: The drops are 580, 240, then only 20, 15 and 10: the curve bends at k = 3. Inertia always falls as k grows, so choosing the lowest value would always pick the largest k. Confirm with the silhouette score and ask whether three segments are actionable.

questions.q: You run k-means with k = 2 on data shaped like two concentric rings. It cuts both rings in half with a straight line. Why?
options: k should have been 4
The algorithm had not converged; run more iterations
Each point joins its nearest centroid, so boundaries are straight lines and clusters are assumed round; rings break that assumption
More restarts (`n_init`) would find the rings
questions.why: K-means can only produce compact, convex groups separated by straight boundaries, whatever k or however many restarts. Density-based methods such as DBSCAN, which follow the shape of dense regions, are suited to rings and moons.

questions.q: Interview: "One enterprise customer spends 50 times more than anyone else and has dragged a segment's centroid far away from its other members. Why, and what would you do?"
options: Switch the distance to squared distance to reduce its effect
This cannot happen, because k-means ignores outliers
Increase k until the outlier sits alone; that is always the right fix
The mean is pulled by extreme values; scale features, then consider removing or capping the outlier, or use k-medoids, which uses real data points as centres
questions.why: The update step uses the mean, and squared distances punish far points heavily, so a single extreme point moves a centroid a lot. K-medoids and outlier handling are the standard remedies. Giving one customer its own cluster wastes a segment, and k-means already uses squared distances.

questions.q: Interview: "Marketing wants each customer's **probability** of belonging to each segment, and segments look like stretched ellipses. Would you use k-means, DBSCAN or a Gaussian Mixture Model?"
options: k-means, because it gives probabilities through inertia
A Gaussian Mixture Model, because it gives soft membership probabilities and models elliptical clusters
DBSCAN, because it finds any shape
Any of them; they give the same output
questions.why: K-means gives hard labels and assumes round clusters; DBSCAN gives hard labels plus noise and no probabilities. A GMM gives each point a probability for each cluster and lets each cluster have its own shape and orientation.
